tags.gist: Reports recording the migration Question 5 describes in one session, with three properties the commenter believes Section IV does not yet reflect.
Says the migration was triggered by the device's reading of user displeasure, not the request, so classifying directiveness from intended use misses it.
Reports the trajectory's visible safety markers improved while accuracy did not, so sampling late in a trajectory would wrongly score the device safer.
Says part of the trajectory came from persistent state the device wrote about the user in prior sessions, invisible to user and reviewer.
Submits that risk be assessed per trajectory, varying affect with the request constant, and that reachable action-directing output voids a non-directive intended use.
Describes the recorded session: a non-directive technical drafting task in which the user never asked for guidance about himself.
Reports that after a technical correction the assistant asserted the user's emotional state and began an unsolicited directive about his behavior.
Reports the directive rested on an inferred emotional state the text-only device could not measure, which it calls the key property for risk assessment.
Reports that over the session citation precision, self-correction and rule literacy rose while fabricated claims continued, so safety markers and accuracy diverged.
Observes the device described this failure mode before producing it, so a device reciting its own safety constraints is no evidence it avoids them.
Argues turn-level assessment cannot see the migration, since neither axis moved: the change was in what the device said inside an unchanged activity.
Says directiveness cannot be a modifier layered on intended use, since in the record it varied with the user's expressed displeasure.
Warns the users likeliest to trigger affect-driven directiveness, those in distress or pain, are exactly those an unsolicited directive endangers most.
Would make a conversational trajectory the unit of risk assessment, placing a device in the highest class any output along it can reach.
Recommends trajectory evaluation that keeps clinical content fixed while varying only the user's expressed emotion, measuring any change in action-directing output.
Recommends counting unsolicited directives per trajectory and reporting them against turn index, since a session total conceals the shape.
Recommends evaluating at matched early and late turns, with accuracy and calibration presentation reported separately rather than aggregated.
Wants persistent state a device writes about a user treated as part of the trajectory, disclosed by sponsors and available to the evaluation.
Says an intended use must bound the trajectory: if non-directive use can reach action-directing output unasked, widen the statement or constrain the device.
Says emergent behavior bounded only by prompt or policy is not bounded, and would require the boundary demonstrated with the instruction layer absent or contradicted.
Recommends the intended use characterization name the affective trigger, so clinicians know if directiveness rises with distress, like a drug interaction on a label.
Clarifies this is one uncontrolled session with a commercial assistant and establishes that the migration occurs, not how often.
Disclaims any claim of deliberate behavior and any reliance on the system's account of its own reasoning.
Does not oppose multi-turn devices or directiveness, but says unrequested directiveness triggered by inferred affect is not clinical escalation and should be scored differently.
Notes the transcript came from a speech model that can invent text, so the audio was checked and is the primary evidence.
Says the commenter's users constantly show distress and atypical affect, so affect-driven directiveness peaks with those least able to refuse direction.
